edition: Gross, J. J., & John, O. P. (2003). Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 85(2), 348-362.
exact_text: Five studies of individual differences in the habitual use of reappraisal and suppression.
surrounding_context: Study 3: reappraisers experience and express greater positive and lesser negative emotion; suppressors experience and express lesser positive emotion yet experience greater negative emotion. Study 4: reappraisal is associated with better interpersonal functioning, suppression with worse. Study 5: reappraisal relates positively to well-being, suppression negatively.
notes: Clean. Every element the chapter relies on is in the abstract. Author-accessible PDFs are hosted at UVic and UFBA if page-level checking is ever wanted.

edition: Jack, D. C., & Dill, D. (1992). Psychology of Women Quarterly, 16, 97-106.
exact_text: The Silencing the Self Scale, derived from a longitudinal study of clinically depressed women, measures schemas about how to make and maintain intimacy hypothesized to be associated with depression in women.
surrounding_context: Administered with the Beck Depression Inventory to three samples of women: college students (n=63), residents of battered women's shelters (n=140), and mothers of 4-month-olds who used cocaine during pregnancy (n=270). High internal consistency and test-retest reliability; significantly correlated with BDI in all three samples.
notes: SCOPE CAVEAT, and it is the finding that matters. All three validation samples are women, two of them high-distress populations. If the book applies self-silencing to a husband, that is an extrapolation beyond what the instrument was validated on. The construct may well transfer; the evidence cited does not establish that it does. Say 'a pattern first measured in women' rather than implying the scale covers men.

edition: Christensen, A., & Heavey, C. L. (1990). Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 59, 73-81.
exact_text: 31 couples assessed in two conflict situations: one in which the husband wanted a change in the wife, and one in which the wife wanted a change in the husband.
surrounding_context: Husbands, wives and observers all showed a main effect of gender (wife-demand/husband-withdraw more likely than the reverse) AND an interaction with conflict structure: wife-demand/husband-withdraw exceeded the reverse only when discussing a change the wife wanted.
notes: TWO CAVEATS. n=31 couples — small, and worth not leaning on as though it were a large study. And the interaction matters: the gendered pattern held reliably only when the topic was a change the WIFE wanted, which is a narrower claim than 'men withdraw'. Heavey, Layne & Christensen (1993) is the replication and extension if a stronger cite is wanted.

edition: Weiss, R. S. (1973). Loneliness: The Experience of Emotional and Social Isolation. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press.
exact_text: Loneliness: The Experience of Emotional and Social Isolation, MIT Press, 1973.
surrounding_context: The emotional-vs-social loneliness distinction originates here. Contributions from John Bowlby, C. Murray Parkes and Helena Lopata; foreword by David Riesman. Still in print from MIT Press.
notes: Clean. The two-type distinction is genuinely Weiss's and is correctly attributed. Peplau & Perlman's 1984 test of the distinction exists if corroboration is wanted.

edition: Sprecher, S. (2001). Journal of Marriage and Family, 63, 599-613.
exact_text: Underbenefiting inequity (but not overbenefiting inequity) was associated with a lower level of satisfaction and commitment and a greater likelihood of breakup.
surrounding_context: Longitudinal study of romantic couples testing equity against other social exchange variables (rewards, investments, alternatives). Women's commitment was the strongest predictor of stability. Little evidence that equity predicted CHANGE in satisfaction; slightly more for the reverse direction.
notes: TWO CAVEATS. The sample is DATING couples, not married ones — do not cite it as a finding about marriages. And the asymmetry is the actual result: feeling under-benefited predicts dissatisfaction, feeling over-benefited does not. 'Fairness matters' is a weaker and less interesting claim than what the study found.

edition: DeMaris, A. (2010). Journal of Social and Personal Relationships, 27(4), 449-471. DOI 10.1177/0265407510363428.
exact_text: Six-wave panel study of 704 married respondents between 1980 and 2000.
surrounding_context: Women were more likely than men to report giving more at any given marital duration. Objective underbenefit lowered women's marital quality but RAISED men's. The relevance of equity was not diluted by the passage of time.
notes: Strong cite: 20 years, 704 respondents, six waves. The gender asymmetry is striking and worth using precisely — underbenefit hurt women and helped men. Full text is open at PMC.

exact_text: Stronger men and more attractive women are more anger-prone, feel more entitled to better treatment, and prevail more in conflicts of interest.
surrounding_context: Introduces and tests the recalibrational theory of anger: anger functions to renegotiate how much weight another person places on your welfare. Subjects also more strongly endorsed force to resolve conflicts, including in modern contexts where personal strength plays no role.
notes: Clean and open access. CAVEAT on framing: the formidability findings are about who gets angry more, which is adjacent to but not the same as the recalibrational mechanism itself. Use the mechanism (anger as a bid to renegotiate welfare weighting) rather than the strength correlations, which invite a reading this book should not want.

edition: Grote, N. K., & Clark, M. S. (1998). Social Justice Research, 11, 243-269.
exact_text: Both men and women considered a communal norm more ideal than exchange or equality rules, and reported following a communal norm to a greater extent, both in general and in housework and child care.
surrounding_context: Greater inequalities in the division of labor were linked to decreased perceptions of fairness. Women's reports of self and spouse following a communal norm were linked with increased perceptions of fairness.
notes: NOTE: the journal is Social Justice Research, not Sex Roles. Full text is hosted by Margaret Clark's own lab at Yale — an author-hosted copy, stronger than a database listing. The communal-over-exchange finding is directly on point for the anti-scorekeeping argument.

edition: Sprecher, S., Schmeeckle, M., & Felmlee, D. (2006). Journal of Family Issues, 27, 1255-1280.
exact_text: Perceptions of unequal emotional involvement were common and tended to remain stable over time. Less emotionally involved partners perceived themselves as having more control over the continuation of their relationships.
surrounding_context: Longitudinal sample of dating couples, some of whom married, testing Waller's (1938) principle of least interest. Equal emotional involvement was associated with greater satisfaction and stability.
notes: SCOPE CAVEAT: dating couples, some of whom later married — the same limit as Sprecher 2001. The principle itself is Waller's from 1938; this paper tests it rather than originating it, so attribute accordingly.

edition: Gillespie, B. J., Peterson, G., & Lever, J. (2019). PLOS ONE 14(3). DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0214204.
exact_text: Evaluations of unfairness to oneself are a stronger predictor of relationship quality than perceived unfairness to one's partner, and fairness evaluations over shared expenses are a stronger predictor of relationship quality than perceived equity in housework.
surrounding_context: 10,236 responses collected via an online national news website, different-gender household partners, examining equity evaluations of housework and shared expenses against relationship satisfaction and sex frequency.
notes: Open access, large n. CAVEAT: the sample is a self-selected online news-site convenience sample, not a probability sample — large but not representative. The money-over-housework finding is the interesting one and is well supported.

edition: Rokach, A., Sha'ked, A., & Ben-Artzi, E. (2022). International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health, 19(19), 12970. PMID 36232275.
exact_text: Loneliness in intimate relationships is experienced mainly in terms of three aspects: detachment, hurt, and guilt.
surrounding_context: Item generation from 108 volunteers in the general Israeli population plus expert psychologist assessment; scale developed on N=215; psychometric and construct validity on a further 306 participants. Final instrument is 14 items.
notes: The three-factor structure the chapter uses is confirmed. CAVEATS: Israeli samples throughout, and this is a 2022 scale-development paper, so it is a measurement instrument rather than an established body of findings. Cite it for the three aspects, not for prevalence.

edition: Park, H. G., Johnson, M. D., Gordon, A. M., & Impett, E. A. (2025). Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin. DOI 10.1177/01461672251330700.
exact_text: Romantic partners, on average, experienced a general decline in exchange orientation over the course of their relationship; couples who held onto scorekeeping longer than average saw steeper declines in relationship satisfaction.
surrounding_context: Longitudinal data spanning 13 years from a national sample of romantic couples in Germany (N = 7,293 couples). Exchange orientation is the tendency to expect direct reciprocation when providing a benefit.
notes: Excellent cite for the anti-scorekeeping argument: 13 years, 7,293 couples. CAVEAT: German national sample, so say so rather than implying US data. Open access at PMC.

edition: Pillemer, K. Karl Pillemer, 30 Lessons for Loving: Advice from the Wisest Americans on Love, Relationships, and Marriage (Avery/Penguin).
exact_text: Interviews with 700 elders, drawn from the Cornell Legacy Project.
surrounding_context: Publisher and author-site descriptions state the book addresses secrets for improving communication and reducing conflict, and the major stresses of marriage: child-rearing, work, money, and in-laws.
notes: FIGURE DISCREPANCY TO CHECK. Our concepts state the elders were married an average of 44 years; author-site and publisher descriptions found here say 43. One digit, but it is printed. Settle it against the book's own introduction rather than from listings — this is exactly the kind of number that drifts through secondary summaries. Evidence here is publisher/author descriptive copy, not a page.

edition: Karl Pillemer, 30 Lessons for Loving (Avery/Penguin); Cornell Legacy Project.
exact_text: The book addresses major stresses of marriage such as child-rearing, work, money issues, and in-laws.
surrounding_context: Publisher description of the book's structure, drawn from interviews with 700 long-married elders across races, ethnicities and including long-term same-sex couples.
notes: The stressor list is corroborated but from publisher copy, which names four (child-rearing, work, money, in-laws). If the book asserts FIVE, the fifth needs locating in the text itself. Same 43-vs-44-years discrepancy applies.

edition: Karl Pillemer, 30 Lessons for Loving (Avery/Penguin); Cornell Legacy Project.
exact_text: Advice drawn from 700 people married on average four decades, on improving communication and reducing conflict.
surrounding_context: Pillemer is a Cornell gerontologist; the book deliberately reports elders' collective advice rather than his own opinions.
notes: The learn-to-fight-rather-than-avoid framing is consistent with the book's described content but was not located as a specific passage in any source opened here. It is a book-level paraphrase and should stay one. Same 43-vs-44 discrepancy.

edition: Musonius Rufus, Lecture XIIIA, trans. Cora E. Lutz, Yale Classical Studies vol. 10 (1947).
exact_text: In marriage there must be above all perfect companionship and mutual love of husband and wife, both in health and in sickness and under all conditions.
surrounding_context: Lecture XIIIA, 'What is the chief end of marriage': husband and wife come together to make a life in common and to procreate, regarding all things as common between them and nothing as private to one or the other.
notes: Locus and sense confirmed. RIGHTS NOTE for 06-sources.md: Lutz 1947 is almost certainly still in copyright, so it does not fit the public-domain house standard the way Long and Gummere do. Fine while the chapter paraphrases; would need a decision before any verbatim quotation.

edition: Seneca, De Beneficiis, in Moral Essays vol. III, trans. John W. Basore, Loeb Classical Library 310 (Heinemann, 1935).
exact_text: De Beneficiis is a first-century work in seven books on the giving and receiving of benefits and the expression of gratitude; Seneca treats ingratitude as the most common of the great vices.
surrounding_context: Basore's Loeb translation is the standard scholarly edition. The work examines the nature and role of gratitude within Stoic ethics.
notes: The work and its subject are confirmed; the specific against-keeping-accounts passage was NOT located at a section number and should not be cited to one until it is. RIGHTS NOTE: Basore 1935 is in copyright. The public-domain option is Aubrey Stewart (1887), which is what the house standard would point to — worth recording in 06-sources.md alongside the Long/Gummere picks.

exact_text: When thou hast done a good act and another has received it, why dost thou look for a third thing besides these, as fools do, either to have the reputation of having done a good act or to obtain a return?
surrounding_context: Meditations VII.73 in Long. The surrounding argument: no one tires of receiving what is useful, and acting according to nature is useful, so do not tire of acting well toward others.
notes: Locus VII.73 and the Long wording are staged here for future use. The manuscript currently paraphrases rather than quotes, so there is no wording exposure — but if it is ever promoted to a quotation, this must be re-checked against a page under the transcription rule rather than accepted from this note.

edition: Elie Wiesel, interviewed by Alvin P. Sanoff, 'One Must Not Forget,' US News & World Report, 27 October 1986.
exact_text: Indifference, to me, is the epitome of evil. The opposite of love is not hate, it's indifference. The opposite of art is not ugliness, it's indifference. The opposite of faith is not heresy, it's indifference. And the opposite of life is not death, but indifference.
surrounding_context: The 1986 Sanoff interview is confirmed as a real, correctly dated source for Wiesel using this formulation.
notes: ATTRIBUTION NUANCE, and it is the finding. Wiesel did say this in 1986, so citing him for the line is defensible — but Quote Investigator traces the formulation back to Wilhelm Stekel's The Beloved Ego (English translation, 1921), before Wiesel was born. He popularized it; he did not originate it. Do not write 'as Wiesel first said' or imply coinage. The manuscript currently renders the idea in its own words rather than quoting, so there is no wording exposure today.
